sources.title: List of Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monuments in Downtown Los Angeles

stops.name: Walt Disney Concert Hall
stops.description: Frank Gehry's billowing steel concert hall opened in 2003 and is the home of the Los Angeles Philharmonic.

stops.name: The Broad
stops.description: Eli and Edythe Broad spent 140 million dollars on this museum for their own collection, then made the permanent galleries free.

stops.name: Los Angeles City Hall
stops.description: Finished in 1928, it was the tallest building in the city until 1966 and is still the tallest base isolated structure in the world.

stops.name: Cathedral of Saint Vibiana
stops.description: Opened in 1876, this was the Catholic cathedral of Los Angeles for more than a century and is now a secular events venue.

stops.name: Continental Building
stops.description: Completed in 1903 as the Braly Block, it was the city's first high rise and stayed its tallest commercial building for fifty three years.

stops.name: The Last Bookstore
stops.description: California's largest new and used bookstore fills a former bank, and the old vault is now one of the rooms you browse.

stops.name: Los Angeles Stock Exchange Building
stops.description: Three carved panels on the granite front stand for finance, production and research, above a trading floor that ran from 1931 to 1986.

stops.name: Los Angeles Central Library
stops.description: Bertram Goodhue designed this 1926 landmark, the main branch of the third largest public library collection in the country.

stops.name: The Biltmore Los Angeles
stops.description: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences was founded at a 1927 luncheon in this hotel, which went on to host eight Oscar ceremonies downstairs.

stops.name: Pershing Square
stops.description: Dedicated in 1866 as La Plaza Abaja, this single block of park took the name of General John J. Pershing in 1918.

stops.name: James Oviatt Building
stops.description: The doors, chandeliers and elevator panels of this 1928 tower are molded glass by Rene Lalique, shipped in from France.

stops.name: Los Angeles Theatre
stops.description: Charlie Chaplin helped pay to finish this movie palace in under six months so it could open with the premiere of City Lights in 1931.

stops.name: Palace Theatre
stops.description: Opened in 1911 for vaudeville, it is the oldest theater left on Broadway and the oldest surviving original Orpheum house in the country.

stops.name: Pacific Electric Building
stops.description: Red Cars rolled out of this 1905 terminal across the whole basin, and Cole's has been serving on the ground floor since 1908.

stops.name: Eastern Columbia Building
stops.description: Turquoise terra cotta and a four sided neon clock tower, granted an exemption from the city height limit, make this 1930 department store the landmark you spot from the freeway.

note: Fifteen stops in a walkable loop of roughly a mile and a quarter: Bunker Hill down Grand, across the Civic Center, then south through the Historic Core on Spring, Broadway and Main. Every stop has its own English Wikipedia article, and every one carries coordinates from that article. ZIPs were looked up per address against the Census geocoder and cross checked against Nominatim; where the two disagreed I took the Census answer, except for the Central Library, where the library's own site gives 90071. Deliberately skipped because public.waypoints already holds them for Los Angeles: Angels Flight, the Bradbury Building, the Million Dollar Theatre, Grand Central Market and MOCA Grand Avenue. Those five were my first picks, so this batch is the second fifteen rather than the first, and it still sits in the same walkable core. Dropped Clifton's Cafeteria, which closed in 2018, and Bunker Hill Steps, whose Wikipedia title redirects to the Boston monument. The Palace Theatre is 636 S Broadway per its article, though the marquee and most listings say 630; both addresses geocode to the same building.
